knowledge.title: Transitional governments and the Islamic Courts, 2000–2012 (Dawladihii ku-meelgaarka)
knowledge.text:
Arta conference and TNG (2000): the Somali National Peace Conference in Arta, Djibouti, created the Transitional National Government (TNG) with Abdiqasim Salad Hassan (Cabdiqaasim Salaad Xasan) as president. It introduced the "4.5" clan power-sharing formula for parliament. The TNG never controlled much territory and was opposed by many factions.

TFG (2004): after talks in Kenya (Eldoret and Mbagathi, 2002–2004), the Transitional Federal Government (TFG) was formed with a Transitional Federal Charter, a 275-member parliament selected on the 4.5 formula, and Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed (Cabdullaahi Yuusuf Axmed), former Puntland president, as president. The TFG initially sat in Nairobi, then Jowhar and Baydhabo.

Islamic Courts Union (2006): a coalition of sharia courts, the Islamic Courts Union (ICU, Midowga Maxaakiimta Islaamiga), defeated a US-backed warlord alliance and took Mogadishu in June 2006, bringing a period of relative order; it was led by Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys. Its hardline youth wing, al-Shabaab, later became an independent militant group. In December 2006 Ethiopian forces, supporting the TFG, intervened and ousted the ICU. The African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) deployed from March 2007, with Ugandan troops first, later joined by Burundi, Kenya, Ethiopia, Djibouti and Sierra Leone.

Insurgency and new leadership (2007–2009): an insurgency by al-Shabaab and other groups against Ethiopian and TFG forces caused mass displacement from Mogadishu. Talks in Djibouti (2008) brought moderate ICU leaders into the TFG. Abdullahi Yusuf resigned in December 2008, and Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed was elected president in January 2009 in Djibouti after the parliament was doubled to 550 members; Ethiopian troops withdrew in early 2009.

Turning point (2011–2012): AMISOM and TFG forces pushed al-Shabaab out of Mogadishu in August 2011. Kenya intervened in southern Somalia in October 2011 ("Operation Linda Nchi"), and Kismaayo was taken from al-Shabaab in 2012. A severe famine in 2011 killed an estimated 260,000 people, half of them children under five. Piracy off Somalia peaked around 2009–2011 before declining due to naval patrols and onshore measures.

End of transition: a roadmap led to a Provisional Constitution adopted by a National Constituent Assembly on 1 August 2012, a new Federal Parliament selected by clan elders, and the election of Hassan Sheikh Mohamud as president on 10 September 2012, ending the transitional period.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitional_National_Government; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitional_Federal_Government; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Courts_Union; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union_Mission_to_Somalia

knowledge.title: The Federal Government of Somalia, 2012–2022 (Dawladda Federaalka)
knowledge.text:
The Federal Government of Somalia (FGS, Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya) was established in August–September 2012 under the Provisional Constitution, the first permanent central government since 1991. It was recognised by the United States and others in 2013, reopening embassies over the following years.

Structure: a bicameral Federal Parliament (Golaha Shacabka, the House of the People, with 275 members; and Aqalka Sare, the Upper House, with 54 senators representing federal member states, created in 2016); a president elected by parliament; a prime minister appointed by the president and approved by parliament; and federal member states (dowlad-goboleedyo). MPs have been selected through an indirect clan-based system in which elders choose delegates who elect MPs, with the 4.5 formula guiding seat allocation.

Presidents and key events:
- Hassan Sheikh Mohamud (Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud), 2012–2017: formation of the federal member states (Jubaland 2013, South West 2014, Galmudug 2015, Hirshabelle 2016), a "New Deal" compact with donors (2013), and the gradual expansion of AMISOM operations.
- Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed "Farmaajo" (Maxamed Cabdullaahi Farmaajo), 2017–2022: elected in February 2017. His period included the Zoobe junction truck bombing in Mogadishu on 14 October 2017, which killed more than 500 people, the deadliest attack in Somali history; progress toward debt relief (HIPC decision point in March 2020); tensions with Puntland and Jubaland; and a crisis in April 2021 when parliament extended his term by two years, leading to armed clashes in Mogadishu; the extension was reversed and indirect elections were held in 2021–2022.
- Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was elected again on 15 May 2022, defeating Farmaajo in a parliamentary vote, becoming the first Somali president to win two non-consecutive terms.

Security: AMISOM was replaced by the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) in April 2022, with a plan to hand security to Somali forces. Somali troops were trained by partners including Turkey (TURKSOM base in Mogadishu, opened 2017), the US, UK, UAE, Qatar, Egypt and Eritrea.

Economy and governance: with IMF programmes, Somalia rebuilt public finance, launched a national ID agency, and passed laws on elections and political parties, although one-person-one-vote national elections were repeatedly postponed.

Assistant guidance: give office holders with dates; for anything current, add "as of" dates and check recent news.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Government_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Constitution_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Abdullahi_Mohamed; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14_October_2017_Mogadishu_bombings

knowledge.title: Somaliland: self-declared republic, stated neutrally (Somaliland)
knowledge.text:
Somaliland (Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland) is a territory in the north-west of the Somali peninsula, corresponding to the former British Somaliland Protectorate. It declared independence from Somalia on 18 May 1991, after the fall of Siad Barre, describing it as a restoration of the sovereignty it briefly held from 26 June 1960 until union with Somalia on 1 July 1960. Its capital is Hargeysa; other major towns are Burco, Berbera, Boorama, Ceerigaabo and Laascaanood (the latter now outside its control).

International status (as of October 2026): Somaliland functions as a de facto state with its own government, army, police, currency (the Somaliland shilling) and passports. For more than three decades no UN member recognised it. On 26 December 2025, Israel became the first UN member state to formally recognise Somaliland and establish diplomatic relations; Somaliland's President visited Israel in June 2026 and opened an embassy in Jerusalem. The Federal Government of Somalia rejected the recognition as a violation of its sovereignty, and many countries, the African Union and the Arab League said they continue to support Somalia's territorial integrity. Taiwan and Somaliland have exchanged representative offices since 2020. In January 2024 Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum of understanding on sea access at Berbera in exchange for possible recognition, causing a major diplomatic crisis with Somalia; Turkey mediated the Ankara Declaration between Somalia and Ethiopia in December 2024.

Politics: Somaliland has a presidential system with an elected House of Representatives and an unelected House of Elders (Golaha Guurtida). Only three national political parties are allowed at a time. Presidents have included Abdirahman Ahmed Ali Tuur, Mohamed Haji Ibrahim Egal, Dahir Riyale Kahin, Ahmed Mohamed Silanyo and Muse Bihi Abdi. In the presidential election of 13 November 2024, opposition candidate Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi "Cirro" (Waddani party) won about 64% of the vote and took office in December 2024, a peaceful transfer widely praised by observers.

Conflict in the east: in 2023, fighting in Laascaanood between Somaliland forces and SSC-Khaatumo forces ended with Somaliland's withdrawal from the area; the region later became the federally recognised North East State.

How to discuss it: Somaliland's status is disputed. Use neutral wording such as "Somaliland, which declared independence in 1991 and is recognised by Israel but claimed by Somalia as part of its territory". Do not tell users that Somaliland "is" or "is not" a country as your own position; report what each side says. Respect users' own terms: many in Somaliland say "Somaliland" and "Hargeysa is our capital", while many other Somalis say "Waqooyi" (the North) or "gobollada waqooyi".
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somaliland; https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4g417md05go; https://www.gov.il/en/pages/israel-recognizes-the-republic-of-somaliland-as-an-independent-and-sovereign-state-26-dec-2025; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Somaliland_presidential_election

knowledge.title: Puntland and the federal member states (Puntland iyo dowlad-goboleedyada)
knowledge.text:
Somalia's federal system consists of the Federal Government in Mogadishu and federal member states (dowlad-goboleedyo, FMS). The capital Mogadishu (Banaadir region) has a special status under a governor-mayor, and Somaliland is claimed by the federal government as a member territory although it governs itself separately.

Federal member states (as of October 2026):
- Puntland (Dowladda Puntland ee Soomaaliya): founded 1 August 1998; capital Garoowe; commercial port Boosaaso; regions Bari, Nugaal, northern Mudug, and parts of Sool and Sanaag (contested). President Said Abdullahi Deni (Saciid Cabdullaahi Deni), re-elected January 2024. Puntland suspended recognition of the federal government in March 2024 over constitutional amendments, and in 2026 declared that federal mandates had expired; tensions included clashes in Gaalkacyo in August 2026. Puntland held its first local one-person-one-vote elections in some districts in 2023.
- Jubaland (Jubbaland): formed 2013; seat Kismaayo; regions Gedo, Middle Jubba and Lower Jubba. President Ahmed Mohamed Islaam "Madobe", in office since 2012/2013 and re-elected by the state parliament in November 2024 in a vote the federal government rejected, leading to clashes in Gedo.
- South West State (Koonfur Galbeed): formed 2014; capital Baydhabo (Baidoa); regions Bay, Bakool, Lower Shabeelle. In March 2026 President Abdiaziz Laftagareen cut ties with Mogadishu and resigned as federal forces entered Baydhabo; Aden Mohamed Nur "Madobe" was elected state president in June 2026.
- Galmudug: formed 2015 (re-formed 2020); capital Dhuusamareeb; regions Galguduud and southern Mudug. After direct state assembly elections (rerun 30 September 2026), the assembly elected Liibaan Ahmed Hassan president on 22 October 2026, succeeding Ahmed Abdi Kaariye "Qoorqoor".
- Hirshabelle: formed 2016; capital Jowhar; regions Hiiraan and Middle Shabeelle. President Ali Abdullahi Hussein "Guudlaawe" (since 2020) was nominated by the ruling party for another term after the state's first direct assembly elections on 30 September 2026.
- North East State (Waqooyi Bari Soomaaliya): formerly SSC-Khaatumo; recognised by the federal government as a federal member state in April 2025, named North East State in July–August 2025; capital Laascaanood; claims Sool, eastern Sanaag and Buuhoodle (Cayn). President Abdikhadir Ahmed Aw-Ali "Firdhiye", inaugurated January 2026. Puntland and Somaliland both contest parts of its territory.

Note that boundaries between member states, and between them and Somaliland, are disputed in several places, and relations between Mogadishu and Puntland and Jubaland are tense (as of October 2026). Leaders change frequently; an assistant should verify current office holders before stating them.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Member_States_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puntland; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_State_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_in_Somalia

knowledge.title: Al-Shabaab: factual overview (Xarakada Al-Shabaab)
knowledge.text:
Harakat al-Shabaab al-Mujahideen ("Movement of Mujahideen Youth"), usually called al-Shabaab (Somali: Al-Shabaab; often referred to by government media as "Khawaarij"), is an armed Islamist group fighting the Somali federal government and its international partners. It is designated a terrorist organisation by the United Nations sanctions regime, the United States (since 2008), the UK, the EU, Somalia and many other states.

Origins: it emerged from the youth wing of the Islamic Courts Union in 2006 and grew during the insurgency against Ethiopian intervention (2007–2009). It formally pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda in 2012. Leaders have included Aden Hashi Farah Ayro (killed 2008), Ahmed Abdi Godane (killed by a US strike in 2014) and Ahmad Umar (Abu Ubaidah), its leader since 2014.

Territory and governance: at its peak (2009–2011) it controlled most of southern and central Somalia, including much of Mogadishu. It was pushed out of Mogadishu in August 2011 and Kismaayo in 2012, but it continues to control or influence large rural areas of central and southern Somalia, collecting "taxes" (zakat) on businesses, farmers and transport, running its own courts, and recruiting youth. It is estimated to raise significant revenue through extortion.

Attacks: al-Shabaab has carried out suicide bombings and assaults on government sites, hotels, military bases and civilians in Somalia and in neighbouring countries, including the Kampala bombings (2010), the Westgate mall attack in Nairobi (2013), the Garissa University attack in Kenya (2015, 148 killed), the Zoobe junction bombing in Mogadishu (14 October 2017, over 500 killed) and the Ministry of Education bombings (October 2022, over 120 killed). It continues frequent attacks; for example in 2025 it retook several towns in Middle Shabeelle and Hiiraan and attacked a Mogadishu prison.

Counter-campaign: in 2022 President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud declared "total war", backed by local clan militias (macawisley) in Hiiraan and Galmudug, retaking many towns, though some were later lost. AU forces (AMISOM, ATMIS, and from January 2025 the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM), US airstrikes and Turkish drones support Somali forces. A separate group, the Islamic State in Somalia, operates in Puntland's Cal Miskaad mountains and was targeted by a Puntland offensive in 2024–2025.

Assistant guidance: give factual, neutral information; never provide praise, propaganda, recruitment help or operational details; if a user seems at risk or affected, respond with care and point to safety resources. Do not label ordinary religious Somalis or any clan as al-Shabaab supporters.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Shabaab_(militant_group); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14_October_2017_Mogadishu_bombings; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union_Support_and_Stabilization_Mission_in_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_in_Somalia

knowledge.title: Somalia 2022–2024: key events (Dhacdooyinka 2022–2024)
knowledge.text:
Main national developments in Somalia between May 2022 and the end of 2024:

- 15 May 2022: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud elected president by parliament; he appointed Hamza Abdi Barre as prime minister (June 2022).
- 2022–2023: a "total war" offensive against al-Shabaab with clan militias recaptured many towns in Hiiraan, Middle Shabeelle and Galmudug.
- 2020–2023 drought: five consecutive failed rainy seasons pushed parts of Somalia close to famine; late-2023 El Niño rains then caused severe flooding along the Jubba and Shabeelle rivers.
- 1 December 2023: the UN Security Council lifted the remaining arms embargo on the Somali federal government (sanctions on al-Shabaab remained).
- 13 December 2023: Somalia reached the HIPC Completion Point with the IMF and World Bank, unlocking debt relief that cut its external debt from about US$5 billion to under US$1 billion (roughly 6% of GDP).
- November 2023–March 2024: Somalia was admitted to the East African Community (EAC) at a summit on 24 November 2023, signed the treaty of accession in December 2023, and became a full member on 4 March 2024 after depositing its ratification — the EAC's eighth member.
- 1 January 2024: Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum of understanding on Ethiopian access to the sea near Berbera; Somalia called it illegal and a crisis followed, with Egypt and Eritrea aligning with Mogadishu. Turkey mediated the Ankara Declaration between Somalia and Ethiopia on 11 December 2024, restoring relations.
- February 2024: Somalia and Turkey signed a defence and maritime cooperation agreement, including help protecting Somali waters; Turkey also later agreed oil and gas exploration offshore.
- March 2024: parliament approved amendments to the first four chapters of the provisional constitution, strengthening the presidency and providing for direct elections; Puntland withdrew recognition of the federal government in protest (31 March 2024).
- 6 June 2024: Somalia was elected to a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2025–2026, the first time since 1971–1972.
- 13 November 2024: Somaliland held a presidential election won by opposition candidate Abdirahman "Cirro".
- November–December 2024: a dispute over Jubaland's state election led to a break between Jubaland and Mogadishu and clashes in Gedo region.
- 27 December 2024: the UN Security Council authorised AUSSOM to replace ATMIS from 1 January 2025.

These are documented historical facts; for interpretation (e.g. whether constitutional changes were legitimate), present each side's position.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_Somalia; https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2023/12/13/pr23438-somalia-imf-and-world-bank-announce-somalia-reaches-hipc-completion-point; https://www.eac.int/press-releases/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Somaliland_Memorandum_of_Understanding

knowledge.title: Somalia 2025–2026: key events and the election dispute (Dhacdooyinka 2025–2026)
knowledge.text:
Main developments in Somalia from January 2025 to October 2026 (as of 22 October 2026; verify for later changes):

2025:
- 1 January 2025: AUSSOM (African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia) replaced ATMIS. Somalia began its 2025–2026 term on the UN Security Council.
- Al-Shabaab offensives in 2025 retook several towns in Middle Shabeelle and Hiiraan (e.g. Adan Yabaal, Moqokori); a bomb attack targeted the president's convoy in Mogadishu on 18 March 2025, which he survived.
- April–August 2025: the federal government recognised SSC-Khaatumo as a federal member state (April 2025); it adopted the name North East State in July–August 2025.
- May 2025: President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud launched the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP).
- June 2025: the US barred entry of Somali nationals under a travel proclamation.
- 25 December 2025: Mogadishu held direct local council elections, the first direct vote in the capital since 1969.
- 26 December 2025: Israel recognised Somaliland, which Somalia condemned.

2026:
- January 2026: the US suspended assistance to the federal government over aid-diversion allegations; Somalia cancelled all its agreements with the UAE (12 January); the North East State president was inaugurated in Laascaanood.
- 4 March 2026: the federal parliament approved a new completed constitution providing for direct elections, a multiparty system, and five-year terms for the president and parliament. The opposition Somali Future Council, Puntland and Jubaland rejected it; a challenge was filed at the Supreme Court.
- March 2026: South West State's president cut ties with Mogadishu and resigned as federal forces took Baydhabo; Aden Madobe was elected South West president in June 2026.
- 15 May 2026: the end date of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's original four-year term. The government says the amended constitution extends terms to five years and declared a transition period; the opposition and Puntland say his mandate expired. UK- and US-mediated talks collapsed.
- September–October 2026: first direct state assembly and local council elections in Hirshabelle and a rerun in Galmudug (30 September); the JSP won large majorities; Galmudug's assembly elected Liibaan Ahmed Hassan president on 22 October 2026.
- 15 October 2026: the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (NIEBC) scheduled one-person-one-vote federal parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and the presidential election for 15 May 2027, with voter and party registration from 1 to 22 November 2026. The opposition rejects the process.
- Other: piracy resurged off Puntland in 2025–2026; in April 2026 Somalia registered its first national-flagged ship since 1991; the Central Bank continued preparing new Somali shilling banknotes.

Assistant guidance: the legitimacy of the term extension is disputed; describe the government's and the opposition's positions without endorsing either. Always state "as of" dates.

knowledge.title: Geography of Somalia: overview (Juqraafiga Soomaaliya)
knowledge.text:
Somalia (Soomaaliya; officially the Federal Republic of Somalia, Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya) occupies the eastern tip of the Horn of Africa (Geeska Afrika). It borders Djibouti to the north-west, Ethiopia to the west, and Kenya to the south-west, with the Gulf of Aden (Gacanka Cadmeed) to the north and the Indian Ocean (Badweynta Hindiya) to the east. Including Somaliland, the country covers about 637,657 km², and it has the longest coastline of mainland Africa, about 3,333 km. Raas Caseyr (Cape Guardafui) marks the tip of the Horn at the entrance to the Gulf of Aden, and Raas Xaafuun (Ras Hafun) further south is the easternmost point of mainland Africa.

Landscape: the north has a narrow, hot coastal plain (the Guban, "burnt land") along the Gulf of Aden, behind which rise the Golis and Cal Madow mountains and the Ogo highlands. The highest point is Shimbiris (Shimbiris), about 2,400 m, near Ceerigaabo in Sanaag, in the area of the Daallo forest. South of the mountains lie plateaus such as the Haud (Hawd) and Sool, used for grazing. Central Somalia is mostly semi-arid plains and dunes (Mudug, Galguduud). The south contains the country's only permanent rivers, the Jubba and the Shabeelle, with fertile farmland between them in the Bay, Lower Shabeelle and Jubba regions. The coast has fishing towns, mangroves in the far south, and the Bajuni Islands near Kismaayo.

Population: UN estimates put Somalia's population at around 18–19 million (2024–2025), very young (median age around 16–17), and growing about 3% a year. A large share are pastoralists or agro-pastoralists, but urbanisation is fast, with Mogadishu the largest city. Millions are internally displaced (IDPs, barakacayaal), mostly living around cities due to conflict, drought and floods.

Time and codes: Somalia uses East Africa Time (UTC+3), no daylight saving. Country calling code +252; internet domain .so; ISO code SO/SOM. Driving is on the right.

Natural resources: livestock rangeland, fisheries (among the richest waters in the western Indian Ocean), frankincense and myrrh trees, bananas and other crops along the rivers, and potential offshore and onshore oil and gas (exploration licences signed with Turkey's TPAO and others; Puntland has had onshore exploration). Environmental challenges include recurrent drought, floods, deforestation for charcoal, desertification and coastal erosion.

Assistant guidance: when a user mentions a place, use the official Somali spelling and give the common English form (e.g. Muqdisho/Mogadishu, Kismaayo/Kismayo, Baydhabo/Baidoa).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia; https://population.un.org/wpp/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimbiris

knowledge.title: Regions of Somalia (Gobollada Soomaaliya) and their capitals
knowledge.text:
Somalia is formally divided into 18 administrative regions (gobollo), a structure dating from the 1980s and still used by the federal government, statistics and aid agencies. Each region is divided into districts (degmooyin). The regions with their capitals and the federal member state or administration that governs most of each (as of October 2026; boundaries are disputed in places):

North-west (administered by Somaliland, which has created additional regions of its own):
1. Awdal – Boorama
2. Woqooyi Galbeed (Somaliland calls it Maroodi Jeex) – Hargeysa
3. Togdheer – Burco
North / disputed between Somaliland, Puntland and the North East State:
4. Sanaag – Ceerigaabo
5. Sool – Laascaanood (North East State capital)
North-east (Puntland):
6. Bari – Boosaaso (Puntland has also created additional regions of its own; usage varies)
7. Nugaal – Garoowe
Central:
8. Mudug – Gaalkacyo (north Mudug in Puntland, south Mudug in Galmudug)
9. Galguduud – Dhuusamareeb (Galmudug)
10. Hiiraan – Beledweyne (Hirshabelle)
11. Shabeellaha Dhexe (Middle Shabeelle) – Jowhar (Hirshabelle)
Capital:
12. Banaadir – Muqdisho (Mogadishu)
South (South West State):
13. Shabeellaha Hoose (Lower Shabeelle) – Marka
14. Bay – Baydhabo
15. Bakool – Xuddur
South (Jubaland):
16. Gedo – Garbahaarrey
17. Jubbada Dhexe (Middle Jubba) – Bu'aale
18. Jubbada Hoose (Lower Jubba) – Kismaayo

Federal member state capitals: Puntland – Garoowe; Galmudug – Dhuusamareeb; Hirshabelle – Jowhar; South West – Baydhabo; Jubaland – Kismaayo; North East State – Laascaanood. Somaliland's capital is Hargeysa.

Notes: parts of the Jubba, Shabeelle and central regions are controlled or contested by al-Shabaab, so administrative maps do not always reflect control on the ground. Region names are often used for identity and for addresses; there is no national postal code system in practical everyday use, so deliveries rely on landmarks, districts and phone numbers.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Member_States_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_State_of_Somalia

knowledge.title: Major cities of southern and central Somalia: Muqdisho, Kismaayo, Baydhabo, Beledweyne, Jowhar, Marka, Dhuusamareeb, Gaalkacyo
knowledge.text:
Muqdisho (Mogadishu; also called Xamar): capital and largest city, in Banaadir region on the Indian Ocean, with an estimated population of well over two million. Historic districts include Xamar Weyne and Shangaani, the old trading quarters; other districts include Hodan, Wadajir, Waaberi, Dayniile, Kaaraan, Yaaqshiid, Hawl Wadaag, Wardhiigley, Boondheere, Shibis, Cabdicasiis, Dharkenley, Heliwaa and Kaxda. Landmarks: Aden Adde International Airport, the seaport, Lido beach (Liido), Bakaaraha market (the largest market), the Arbaca Rukun and Fakr ad-Din mosques, Villa Somalia (the presidential palace), the National Theatre, Mogadishu Stadium and Tarabuunka square (with the Daljirka Dahsoon, Tomb of the Unknown Soldier). The city has been rebuilding rapidly since 2011, but security incidents still occur.

Kismaayo (Kismayo): port city in Lower Jubba near the mouth of the Jubba River, seat of Jubaland State; known for its port, fishing, livestock and charcoal trade history, and nearby beaches.

Baydhabo (Baidoa): capital of Bay region and of South West State, in the agricultural heartland of the Rahanweyn/Maay-speaking population; sorghum and maize farming; the Maay dialect (Af-Maay) is widely spoken.

Beledweyne (Beledweyn): capital of Hiiraan, on the Shabeelle River near the Ethiopian border; frequently affected by river floods, especially in Gu' and Dayr seasons.

Jowhar (Jawhar): capital of Middle Shabeelle and of Hirshabelle; historically known for the Italian-era sugar plantation and factory, and for irrigated farming along the Shabeelle.

Marka (Merca): historic port in Lower Shabeelle, about 100 km south of Mogadishu, with old stone architecture and a banana-export history; regional capital of Lower Shabeelle.

Dhuusamareeb (Dusmareb): capital of Galguduud and of Galmudug State, in the central semi-arid pastoral zone.

Gaalkacyo (Galkayo): main city of Mudug, an important trade crossroads between the north and south; historically divided between a northern part administered by Puntland and a southern part administered by Galmudug, with periodic tensions.

Other notable towns: Afgooye (Shabeelle farming town, famous for the Istunka festival), Baraawe (historic coastal town with the Chimwiini/Bravanese dialect), Hobyo (historic sultanate port), Ceel Buur, Xuddur, Garbahaarrey, Bu'aale, Jilib and Dhobley (near the Kenyan border).

Assistant guidance: give travel or security advice only from current sources; use local names with English forms.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogadishu; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kismayo; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baidoa; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beledweyne

knowledge.title: Major cities of northern Somalia and Somaliland: Hargeysa, Burco, Berbera, Boosaaso, Garoowe, Ceerigaabo, Laascaanood, Boorama
knowledge.text:
Hargeysa (Hargeisa): capital of Somaliland and the largest city in the north, in the Woqooyi Galbeed/Maroodi Jeex region. It was largely destroyed in the 1988 bombardment and rebuilt since 1991. Landmarks include the MiG fighter-jet monument commemorating the 1988 events, Egal International Airport, the Waaheen market, the large livestock market, and the Hargeysa Cultural Centre, which hosts the annual Hargeysa International Book Fair (since 2008). The Laas Geel rock art site is about 50 km away.

Burco (Burao): second city of Somaliland, capital of Togdheer, on the seasonal Togdheer river; a major livestock trading hub. The 1991 conference that declared Somaliland's independence was held here.

Berbera: historic port on the Gulf of Aden (Saaxil region), with one of the longest runways in Africa, built in the Cold War era. The port was expanded under a DP World concession, including a new terminal opened in 2021, and is linked by the Berbera Corridor road to Ethiopia. Berbera is a key livestock export port, especially to Saudi Arabia before Hajj.

Boosaaso (Bosaso): commercial capital of Puntland and capital of Bari region, a port on the Gulf of Aden; major centre for livestock exports, imports, fishing and trade; Bender Qassim International Airport. Very hot in summer (Xagaa).

Garoowe (Garowe): administrative capital of Puntland in Nugaal region, seat of the Puntland government, parliament and Puntland State University; it has grown rapidly since 1998.

Ceerigaabo (Erigavo): capital of Sanaag region, in the cool highlands near Shimbiris mountain and the Daallo forest; claimed by Somaliland and contested in the region.

Laascaanood (Las Anod): capital of Sool region and of the North East State (formerly SSC-Khaatumo), recognised by the federal government; the scene of fighting in 2023 after which Somaliland forces withdrew. The 2025 conference that established the state was held here.

Boorama (Borama): capital of Awdal region in western Somaliland, near Ethiopia, known for Amoud University and for being the site of the 1993 Borama peace conference.

Other notable places: Saylac (Zeila), an ancient port near Djibouti; Laas Qoray and Maydh on the Sanaag coast; Qardho in Bari; Eyl on the Puntland coast (historic Dervish site, later known for piracy); Taleex (Taleh), the Dervish capital in Sool; Buuhoodle in Cayn; Gabiley, Somaliland's farming area; and Sheekh, a highland town with a famous boarding school.

Assistant guidance: be careful with political labels for contested places (Ceerigaabo, Laascaanood, Buuhoodle); describe who administers or claims them, without taking sides.

knowledge.title: Rivers of Somalia: Jubba and Shabeelle (Webiyada Jubba iyo Shabeelle)
knowledge.text:
Somalia has only two permanent rivers, both of which rise in the Ethiopian highlands and flow south-east into southern Somalia. Together they support most of Somalia's crop farming and a large share of its population.

Jubba (Webiga Jubba, Juba): formed by the Genale (Ganaane) and Dawa rivers, which meet near Doolow on the Ethiopia–Somalia–Kenya border area. It flows south through Gedo (Luuq, Garbahaarrey area, Baardheere), Middle Jubba (Bu'aale, Saakow, Jilib) and Lower Jubba (Jamaame), reaching the Indian Ocean near Goobweyn, just north of Kismaayo. The Jubba carries more water than the Shabeelle and always reaches the sea. Its valley grows maize, sesame, bananas, mangoes, rice and vegetables; the riverine Somali Bantu (Gosha) communities have farmed it for centuries. The Baardheere dam has long been proposed but not built.

Shabeelle (Webiga Shabeelle, Shebelle; "leopard river"): rises in Ethiopia's Bale Mountains, flows through the Somali Region of Ethiopia (Gode/Godey), enters Somalia near Ferfer and Beledweyne (Hiiraan), passes Bulobarde and Jowhar (Middle Shabeelle), then turns south-west parallel to the coast near Balcad and Afgooye, past Qoryooley and into Lower Shabeelle. In most years it does not reach the ocean, ending in swamps and sand near Jilib, close to the Jubba. It is one of Africa's longer rivers at roughly 1,800–2,000 km. Its irrigated land, especially in Lower Shabeelle, is Somalia's breadbasket for maize, sorghum, sesame, bananas, citrus and sugarcane.

Hazards: both rivers flood regularly during the Gu' (April–June) and Dayr (October–December) rains, especially in Beledweyne, Jowhar, Bulobarde, Baardheere, Luuq and Doolow, displacing hundreds of thousands in bad years (e.g. the 2023 El Niño floods). In droughts they can run very low or dry in places. Canal and embankment damage since 1991 has worsened floods. FAO-SWALIM publishes river-level monitoring and flood alerts.

Other water features: seasonal rivers (togg, plural tog) in the north fill after rain, such as the Togdheer, Nugaal valley watercourses (Dooxada Nugaal) and the Darror. Groundwater from wells (ceel) and berkads (berked, cement rainwater cisterns) is crucial for pastoralists.

Assistant guidance: for flood or river conditions, cite current FAO-SWALIM or government alerts, not memory.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubba_River; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shebelle_River; https://www.faoswalim.org/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Somalia

knowledge.title: Climate of Somalia: heat, monsoons, rains and droughts (Cimilada Soomaaliya)
knowledge.text:
Somalia has a mostly hot, arid to semi-arid climate. Temperatures are high year-round, with average daily highs of about 30–40°C in most lowland areas. The hottest places are on the northern Gulf of Aden coast (Berbera, Boosaaso, Saylac), where summer highs often exceed 40–45°C. The highlands of the north (Hargeysa at about 1,300 m, Sheekh, Ceerigaabo and the Golis and Cal Madow mountains) are noticeably cooler, and nights in Jiilaal can be chilly. Mogadishu has a hot, humid coastal climate moderated by sea breezes, with highs around 28–32°C most of the year.

Rainfall is low and unreliable: most of the country receives under 500 mm per year, the north-east and coastal north often under 200 mm, while the southern riverine and Bay areas receive 500–700 mm. Rain falls in two seasons driven by the Indian Ocean monsoon winds: the Gu' (April–June, main rains) and the Dayr (October–December, short rains). The dry seasons are Jiilaal (December/January–March, harshest) and Xagaa (July–September, windy, with light coastal showers in the south). The south-west monsoon (Xagaa) brings strong winds; the north-east monsoon (Jiilaal) is drier.

Climate shocks: Somalia is among the countries most affected by climate change. Major droughts include the 1974–1975 "Dabadheer" drought, 1991–1992 (with famine), 2010–2011 (famine killing an estimated 260,000), 2016–2017, and 2020–2023 (five consecutive failed rainy seasons, the longest on record). Severe floods occurred in 2019, 2023 (El Niño) and other years. Tropical cyclones occasionally strike, such as Cyclone Gati, which hit Puntland in November 2020 as the strongest recorded storm to make landfall in Somalia. Locusts invaded in 2019–2021.

Practical notes: dust storms occur in Xagaa in the north; humidity is high on the coast; heat is dangerous in Jiilaal and Xagaa for the elderly and livestock. Seasonal forecasts and drought assessments are issued by FAO-SWALIM, FSNAU, the Somali Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) and the IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC).

Assistant guidance: for a weather question, use a live forecast for the user's city; for drought or famine status, give current figures from the latest FSNAU/IPC or OCHA reports with "as of" dates.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclone_Gati; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%932023_Horn_of_Africa_drought; https://fsnau.org/

knowledge.title: Somali regions outside Somalia: Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti (Soomaalida Itoobiya, Kenya iyo Jabuuti)
knowledge.text:
Somali people live across the Horn of Africa beyond Somalia's borders, a legacy of colonial partition symbolised by the five-pointed star on the Somali flag.

Ethiopia – Somali Region (Dawlad Deegaanka Soomaalida Itoobiya; also called Soomaali Galbeed or historically the Ogaden): Ethiopia's second-largest regional state by area, in the east and south-east, bordering Somalia, Somaliland, Djibouti and Kenya. Capital: Jigjiga (Jijiga). Other towns: Godey (Gode), Qabridahar (Kebri Dehar), Dhagaxbuur (Degehabur), Wardheer, Doolo, Shilaabo, Dolo Ado, Moyale (shared with Oromia and Kenya). The population is estimated at well over five million, overwhelmingly Somali and mostly pastoral. The region has its own government and uses Somali as its official working language. Its history includes the 1977–1978 Ogaden War, the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) insurgency (which signed a peace deal with Ethiopia in 2018), and severe abuses under former president Abdi Mohamoud Omar (Abdi Iley) before 2018. Ethiopian Somalis are also present in Dire Dawa and Addis Ababa.

Kenya – North Eastern Kenya: the former North Eastern Province, now Garissa, Wajir and Mandera counties, plus Somali communities in Isiolo, Marsabit, Tana River and Nairobi. The 2019 Kenyan census counted about 2.8 million ethnic Somalis. Nairobi's Eastleigh district ("Little Mogadishu") is a major Somali commercial hub. The Dadaab refugee complex near Garissa, opened in 1991, hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees from Somalia. Kenyan Somalis hold prominent positions in Kenyan politics and business. This area was the British "Northern Frontier District", and the 1963–1967 Shifta War followed its inclusion in Kenya.

Djibouti (Jamhuuriyadda Jabuuti): independent since 27 June 1977 (formerly French Somaliland). About 1 million people; Somali (mostly Issa) are the majority, roughly 60%, and Afar about 35%. Official languages are French and Arabic; Somali and Afar are national languages widely spoken. President Ismail Omar Guelleh, in office since 1999, won a sixth term in April 2026 with about 97% of the vote in an election boycotted by the main opposition. Djibouti's port is Ethiopia's main sea outlet, and it hosts military bases of the US, France, China, Japan and Italy. Djibouti hosted the Arta conference (2000) and the 2008–2009 Somali peace talks.

Yemen also has a long-established Somali community and many refugees. Assistant guidance: respect users' own identification ("Soomaali Galbeed", "Kenyan Somali", "Djiboutian"), and don't express positions on border claims.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Region; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Eastern_Province_(Kenya); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djibouti; https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cgj0wg423n6o

knowledge.title: Somali oral poetry: forms and metre (Maansada Soomaaliyeed: gabay, geeraar, jiifto, buraambur, hees)
knowledge.text:
Somalis have been called "a nation of poets" (the phrase is associated with the explorer Richard Burton and later scholars). Poetry (maanso, gabay in the broad sense) was the main medium for news, politics, love, satire, mediation and history, memorised and transmitted orally by reciters (hal-hayeen) before Somali was written in 1972. A poet is an abwaan or gabayaa; a great poet is often called "abwaan".

Main classical genres:
- Gabay: the most prestigious form, long lines in a weighty metre, used for serious topics such as war, politics, philosophy and rebuke. Recited slowly. The Sayid's and Raage Ugaas's most famous poems are gabay.
- Geeraar: shorter lines, a faster, galloping rhythm, traditionally recited on horseback for war, challenges and praise.
- Jiifto: medium-length lines in a lighter metre, used for many topics including conflict and everyday matters; very common in modern poetry.
- Buraambur (buraanbur): the main women's genre, sung with drums and clapping at weddings, celebrations and gatherings, praising the bride, family, community or nation, or commenting on politics.
- Hees (song) and the many work and dance songs: hees hawleed (work songs for watering camels, weaving, pounding grain), hees carruureed (children's songs), cradle songs (hoobeeyo), and dance songs (heello, dhaanto, saar). Modern popular songs are called hees or heeso.
- Other forms include the masafo, the guurow and the wiglo.

Alliteration (higgaad / qaafiyad): the defining rule of Somali poetry is that every line (or half-line) of a poem contains a word beginning with the same sound, chosen for the whole poem, e.g. a poem "in D" or "in G". Maintaining one alliterating sound through a long poem is a mark of skill.

Metre: Somali poetry is quantitative, based on patterns of long and short vowel lengths (moras), not stress. The poet and scholar Maxamed Xaashi Dhamac "Gaarriye" analysed these metrical rules in the 1970s, showing each genre has its own scansion pattern.

Poetic chains (silsilad): poets answer each other in a series of poems on a shared theme and alliteration. Famous chains include the Guba (19th century), the Siinley and the Deelley (1979–1980), a political chain in "D" in which dozens of poets criticised or defended the Siad Barre regime.

Today, poetry thrives on radio, TV, YouTube, TikTok and at events such as the Hargeysa International Book Fair. An assistant can explain genres, help users compose verse (respecting alliteration), and quote short public-domain lines, but should not reproduce long copyrighted modern poems.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_literature; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_poetry; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxamed_Xaashi_Dhamac; B.W. Andrzejewski & I.M. Lewis, Somali Poetry: An Introduction (1964)

knowledge.title: Famous classical Somali poets (Abwaanadii hore): Raage Ugaas, the Sayid, Ismaaciil Mire, Salaan Carrabey, Cilmi Boodhari
knowledge.text:
Classical Somali poets are household names, and their lines are quoted as proverbs.

Raage Ugaas Warfaa (18th–19th century): a celebrated poet and clan leader from the Ogaden region, renowned for wisdom poetry and a famous elegy (baroorodiiq) for his wife, regarded as one of the most moving poems in Somali. He is often cited as a model of eloquence.

Sayid Maxamed Cabdulle Xasan (c. 1856–1920): leader of the Dervish movement and arguably the most famous Somali poet. His gabay poems rallied followers, rebuked opponents, and commented on events, such as his poem on the death of the British officer Richard Corfield at Dul Madoba (1913) and his poem of advice to his horse and companions. His poetry is considered a summit of classical style, though some of it attacked rival clans and is therefore also controversial.

Ismaaciil Mire (1862–1951): a Dervish commander and poet who composed war poetry and later reflective poems; respected for vivid imagery.

Salaan Carrabey (19th century): a poet from the north known for wit and powerful poems in the "Guba" debates with other poets.

Qamaan Bulxan and Cali Dhuux: classical poets known for exchanges in poetic chains.

Cilmi Boodhari (Elmi Boodhari, c. 1908–1941): a poet from Berbera often called the father of modern Somali love poetry. He composed passionate poems for a woman named Hodan whom he could not marry; legend says he died of lovesickness. His style influenced the balwo and heello love songs of the 1940s–50s.

Cabdillaahi Suldaan Timacadde (1920–1973): a nationalist poet famous for the poem recited at the lowering of the British flag in Hargeysa at independence in 1960, celebrating freedom ("Kana siib kana saar" — "take it down, put [ours] up"). He also wrote about unity and later criticised politics.

Faarax Nuur, Xaaji Aadan Axmed "Af-qalooc" and Mahammed Liibaan "Jaangeli" are other names often mentioned.

Women poets: women have always composed, especially buraambur. Well-known names include Xaawo Jibriil (Hawa Jibril) and, in the modern era, singer-poets such as Saado Cali Warsame (1950–2014), who was also a member of parliament. Classical women's poetry is less recorded because collectors focused on men's gabay.

Assistant guidance: when quoting, use only short, well-known lines and attribute them; poems by poets who died more than 70 years ago are generally in the public domain, but recordings and modern collections may be copyrighted.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_literature; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Abdullah_Hassan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmi_Boodhari; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdillahi_Suldaan_Mohammed_Timacade

knowledge.title: Modern Somali poets and writers: Hadraawi, Gaarriye, Cali Sugulle, Xasan Sheekh Muumin and novelists
knowledge.text:
Modern Somali literature flourished from the 1950s, when poetry merged with song, theatre and radio, and especially after Somali became an official written language in 1972.

Maxamed Ibraahim Warsame "Hadraawi" (1943–2022): widely regarded as the greatest Somali poet of the modern era, sometimes called "the Somali Shakespeare". Born near Burco, he worked in Mogadishu as a teacher and lyricist; his love songs, sung by stars like Magool and Maxamed Mooge, became classics. His political poems angered the Barre regime, and he was imprisoned without trial from 1973 to 1978 (including at Qansax Dheere). Major works include the poem "Hooyo" (Mother), contributions to the "Siinley" chain and to the Deelley chain; his collected poems were published as "Hal-karaan" (1993). In 2003 he led a "Peace March" (Socdaalka Nabadda) across Somali regions. He died in Hargeysa on 18 August 2022.

Maxamed Xaashi Dhamac "Gaarriye" (1949–2012): poet and scholar from Hargeysa who discovered and explained the metrical system of Somali poetry; a leading voice of the Deelley chain (1979–1980) against dictatorship. Died in Norway in 2012.

Cali Sugulle Cigaal "Duncarbeed" (1936–2016): poet, playwright and lyricist of many patriotic, social and political songs from the 1950s onward; a prominent figure in Somali theatre and national songs.

Xasan Sheekh Muumin (1930–2008): playwright and composer, author of "Shabeelnaagood" (1968), translated into English as "Leopard Among the Women", a celebrated play about deceit and women's rights.

Other modern poets and lyricists: Cabdi Aadan Xaad "Qays", Maxamed Cabdillaahi "Kariye", Axmed Ismaaciil Diiriye "Qaasim", Abwaan Cabdi Muxumed Amiin, and Xuseen Aw Faarax.

Written prose: the first novel in Somali is generally considered to be "Aqoondarro waa u nacab jacayl" (Ignorance is the enemy of love) by Faarax Maxamed Jaamac Cawl (1974). Other Somali-language novelists include Maxamed Daahir Afrax and Cali Jimcaale Axmed. In other languages: Nuruddin Farah (born 1945), novelist writing in English, winner of the Neustadt International Prize for Literature (1998), author of "Maps" and "Sweet and Sour Milk"; Nadifa Mohamed (British-Somali), shortlisted for the Booker Prize for "The Fortune Men" (2021); poet Warsan Shire (British-Somali), known for "Home" and work featured in Beyoncé's "Lemonade"; and Abdourahman Waberi (Djibouti, in French).

Book culture today: the Hargeysa International Book Fair (since 2008), the Mogadishu Book Fair (since 2015) and Somali publishers such as Ponte Invisibile/Redsea Online and Looh Press.

Assistant guidance: summarise works in your own words; do not reproduce copyrighted texts or lyrics beyond very short quotations.

knowledge.title: Somali music: Qaraami, balwo, heello, Waaberi and famous singers (Muusigga Soomaaliyeed)
knowledge.text:
Somali music is traditionally based on a pentatonic (five-note) scale and closely tied to poetry: the lyricist (abwaan) is as celebrated as the singer (fannaan) and the composer (laxamiste). The main instruments are the kaban (oud, lute), drums (durbaan), and, from the mid-20th century, violins, keyboards, guitars and saxophones.

Origins of modern music:
- Balwo: a short, two-line love song form created in the 1940s, credited to Cabdi Deeqsi "Cabdi Sinimo" from Boorama. Religious leaders initially criticised it as frivolous.
- Heello: balwo developed into the longer heello, the basis of modern Somali song (hees casri ah).
- Qaraami: the classic love-song era of roughly the 1940s–1960s, centred on Hargeysa and Radio Hargeysa (which began broadcasting in the 1940s), with oud-based songs of longing. Qaraami songs remain beloved and are frequently re-recorded. Key figures include the troupe Walaalaha Hargeysa (Hargeysa Brothers), Cali Feiruuz, Maxamed Axmed Kuluc and the oud master Axmed Ismaaciil Xuseen "Xudeydi" (1928–2020), called "the king of the oud", who died in London in April 2020.

National era: after independence, the state supported music. The Waaberi troupe (Kooxda Waaberi, "dawn"), the national artistic group under the Ministry of Information and National Guidance, brought together top singers, poets and musicians in the 1970s–80s, performing at the National Theatre in Mogadishu and touring abroad. Other groups included the Iftiin band and the Dur-Dur Band (1980s Mogadishu funk/disco, later internationally reissued).

Famous singers (Fannaaniinta caanka ah):
- Magool (Xaliimo Khaliif Cumar, 1948–2004): called "the Somali nightingale"; one of the most loved female voices, singing many songs written by Hadraawi.
- Maxamed Mooge Liibaan: a legendary male singer of the Qaraami and later eras.
- Maxamed Saleebaan Tubeec, Xasan Aadan Samatar, Cumar Dhuule, Axmed Mooge Liibaan.
- Female stars: Saado Cali Warsame, Khadra Daahir, Faadumo Qaasim, Sahra Axmed, Maryam Mursal, Hibo Nuura.
- Diaspora and modern: K'naan (Canadian-Somali rapper, "Wavin' Flag" for the 2010 World Cup), Aar Maanta, Sahra Halgan (Somaliland), Nimco Happy, and many TikTok and YouTube artists.

Dances: dhaanto (northern and Ethiopian Somali), niiko (southern), shirib, saylici, belo, the Banaadiri dances and the Istunka stick-fighting festival in Afgooye. Somali music is listened to at weddings, on YouTube, on radio and via apps.

Note that some religious Somalis avoid music; the assistant should not push music recommendations on users who signal this.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magool; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waaberi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_Ismail_Hussein_Hudeidi

knowledge.title: Somali folktales (Sheekooyinka xariirta): Cigaal Shidaad, Dhegdheer, Caraweelo, Wiil Waal
knowledge.text:
Somali folktales (sheeko, sheeko-xariir, plural sheekooyin) were told to children at night, often ending with a moral or a proverb. Summaries of the best-known:

Cigaal Shidaad: a famous trickster and wit, sometimes lazy or greedy, whose humorous stories show cleverness, quick replies and the consequences of greed. Many short anecdotes feature him outsmarting rich men, sultans or his own wife, and his name is used for a cunning person. Stories vary by teller.

Dhegdheer ("Long-ear"): a terrifying cannibal woman with one enormous ear that could hear sounds from far away. In the common version, a mother and her children (or a girl) are pursued by Dhegdheer and escape by crossing a river or valley; Dhegdheer, trying to follow, drowns or is swept away by a flood. The story warns children about strangers and teaches courage and the value of wits.

Caraweelo (Arawelo): a legendary queen said to have ruled in the northern Somali lands in ancient times. In the tale, she resented men's dominance, took power, gave women authority, and punished men harshly; the story says she was eventually overthrown or killed by a grandson or by men who conspired against her. A site in the north is pointed to as her grave, and the legend says men threw stones on it while women laid flowers or green leaves. Today Caraweelo is debated: some see her as a tyrant in a cautionary tale about gender roles, others as a symbol of women's empowerment. Present both interpretations neutrally.

Wiil Waal ("the daring boy"): Garaad Faarax Garaad Xirsi, a wise and bold ruler (sultan) associated with the Jigjiga area, probably around the 16th century. Tales show him testing his subjects' wisdom. In the best-known, he asks his men to bring him the best and worst part of a slaughtered animal; a wise man brings the tongue for both, because the tongue can create peace or cause war. Other stories involve clever solutions to riddles.

Other tales: animal fables featuring the lion (libaax), the foolish and greedy hyena (dhurwaa) and the cunning jackal or fox (dawaco); and stories of wise elders and djinn (jinni). Riddles (hal xidhaale) and tongue twisters are part of the same oral tradition.

Assistant guidance: retell these as summaries in your own words; note that versions differ between regions and families; when telling stories to children, keep frightening details gentle.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_mythology; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arawelo; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhegdheer; https://somali.wdfiles.com/local--files/readings/AhmedMHC.pdf

knowledge.title: Staple Somali dishes (Cuntooyinka Soomaalida): canjeero, bariis, suqaar, muufo, soor, baasto
knowledge.text:
Somali cuisine reflects pastoral life (meat, milk, ghee), farming in the south (sorghum, maize, beans), and centuries of trade with Arabia, India, Persia and Italy (spices, rice, pasta, tea).

Breakfast staples:
- Canjeero (northern word: laxoox): a thin, spongy, slightly sour fermented pancake made from sorghum, corn or wheat flour batter, cooked on one side on a flat pan (daawo). Eaten for breakfast with ghee (subag) and sugar, honey, tea, or with stews (maraq), liver (beer) or suqaar. It is smaller and thinner than Ethiopian injera.
- Malawax: a sweet, thin crêpe-like pancake made with egg, eaten with tea.
- Muufo: a flatbread made from maize, sorghum or wheat, baked in a clay oven (tinaar) or on a pan; common in the south and in Baydhabo; also eaten with stews.
- Sabaayad: a flaky, layered flatbread similar to paratha/chapati.
- Boorash / mishaari: porridge, often for children and new mothers.

Lunch (the main meal, qado):
- Bariis iskukaris (literally "rice cooked together"): spiced rice cooked with onions, garlic, tomato and xawaash spice mix, often with raisins and fried onions on top, served with goat, mutton, chicken or camel meat, and with a banana on the side, a famous Somali habit.
- Baasto (pasta): a legacy of Italian colonisation, especially in the south; spaghetti with suugo (meat sauce) is a lunch staple, again often with banana.
- Soor: a stiff maize-meal porridge (like polenta) eaten in the south with butter, milk or stew.
- Hilib ari (goat meat), hilib geel (camel meat), and fish along the coast (kalluun), especially in Mogadishu, Kismaayo and Boosaaso.

Dinner (casho): usually lighter—canjeero, sabaayad, beans (digir), rice leftovers, or pasta.

Meat specialities:
- Suqaar: small cubes of meat stir-fried with onions, peppers and spices, eaten with canjeero, rice or bread.
- Muqmad / oodkac: dried meat strips fried and preserved in ghee and spices; a traditional travel food and part of wedding xeedho.
- Maraq: meat or vegetable stew/soup.

Spices: xawaash, the Somali spice blend (cumin, coriander, cardamom, black pepper, cinnamon, cloves, turmeric). Basbaas is the green chilli sauce. Milk (caano) from camels (caano geel), goats and cows is central; fermented camel milk (susac) is prized.

Halal rules apply: Somalis eat only halal meat and do not eat pork or drink alcohol. Food is traditionally eaten with the right hand, often from a shared plate.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_cuisine; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canjeero; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xawaash; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muqmad

knowledge.title: Snacks, sweets and drinks: sambuusa, bajiye, xalwo, shaah and Somali tea culture
knowledge.text:
Snacks (cunto fudud):
- Sambuusa: fried triangular pastries filled with spiced minced meat, fish or vegetables; essential during Ramadan afur and at gatherings.
- Bajiye: fried balls of black-eyed bean or lentil batter with onion and chilli, popular in the south.
- Kac kac: fried sweet dough pieces, similar to doughnuts.
- Cambuulo: adzuki beans cooked with butter and sugar, sometimes mixed with rice or corn; a southern dish.
- Buskud (biscuits) and doolsho (cake) served with tea, especially at Eid.

Xalwo (halwa): the iconic Somali sweet, a dense, gelatinous confection made from sugar, cornstarch, ghee, cardamom and nutmeg, sometimes coloured with saffron, cooked for hours with constant stirring. It is served at weddings, Eid and other celebrations, and given as a gift. Diaspora visitors often bring xalwo back from Somalia.

Shaah (tea): tea is the national drink, drunk several times a day. Somali tea (shaah Soomaali) is strong black tea boiled with sugar and spices such as cardamom (heyl), cinnamon (qorfe), cloves (dhego yare) and ginger (sanjabiil). Shaah caddeys is tea with milk (often a lot of sugar and milk); shaah bigeys is black tea without milk. Tea is served in small glasses or cups, with breakfast, after lunch, in the afternoon (often with snacks) and in the evening. Teashops (maqaayad shaah, "fadhi shaah") are social hubs where men gather to discuss news and politics.

Coffee: coffee (bun, qaxwo) has a long history, especially in the north and among communities near Ethiopia. Traditional coffee is roasted at home, sometimes with spices; coffee husks boiled with spices (qishir) are also drunk. In Hargeysa and Mogadishu, modern cafés serving espresso and macchiato (an Italian legacy) are popular with young people.

Juices and milk: fresh fruit juices (mango, papaya, guava, banana, lemon, tamarind) are popular, especially in Ramadan. Camel milk (caano geel) is highly valued for health and taste, and sold fresh in markets and by delivery; fermented camel milk is called susac (or caano dhanaan).

Hospitality customs: a guest is almost always offered tea, and sometimes incense (uunsi) is burned in a censer (dabqaad) to perfume the room. Refusing tea entirely can seem cold; a polite refusal is "Mahadsanid, waan ka dheregsanahay" (thanks, I'm full) or "Allaha ku caafiyo".

Assistant guidance: offer recipes using xawaash and Somali names, give measurements in grams/cups, and remember that alcohol and pork are never part of Somali dishes.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_cuisine; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halwa; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samosa

knowledge.title: Meal times and eating etiquette in Somali homes (Waqtiyada cuntada iyo edebta cunnada)
knowledge.text:
Somali daily meals follow a pattern shaped by work, prayer and heat:

- Quraac (breakfast): early morning after Subax prayer, typically canjeero/laxoox, sabaayad or malawax with tea, liver, or suqaar.
- Qado (lunch): the main and largest meal, eaten between about 12:30 and 2:30 pm, after Duhur prayer: rice or pasta with meat, salad and banana. Many businesses slow down after lunch, and an afternoon rest is common in hot weather.
- Shaaha galabta (afternoon tea): around Casar time, tea with snacks such as sambuusa, buskud or popcorn.
- Casho (dinner): lighter, typically after Maqrib or Cishe prayer (7–9 pm): canjeero, beans, rice or pasta leftovers, or milk.

During Ramadan the pattern changes to suxuur before dawn and afur at sunset (see the Ramadan entry).

Eating etiquette:
- Say "Bismillaah" before eating and "Alxamdulillaah" after.
- Wash hands before and after meals; in many homes a jug (kildhi) and basin are brought to guests.
- Eat with the right hand; the left hand is not used for eating or passing food.
- Food is often shared from a large common platter (sixni / tobosho), each person eating from the part in front of them. Taking the best meat for yourself is impolite; the host or elders often hand choice pieces to guests.
- Men and women often eat separately at gatherings, though families eat together at home in many households.
- Guests are urged to eat more ("Cun, cun!"), and leaving a little food can signal you are satisfied.
- Wasting food is disliked; leftovers are shared or given away.
- Eating while walking in public is uncommon among older people.

Hospitality: guests are fed generously, even by poor families; a common saying holds that the guest brings blessing. Visitors may bring sugar, tea, fruit or sweets as a gift (hadiyad).

Restaurants: urban Somalis eat out in restaurants serving rice and meat, fish, pasta and Italian-influenced dishes, and in cafés; in the diaspora, Somali restaurants are community hubs. Food delivery apps and phone orders are growing in Mogadishu and Hargeysa.

Assistant guidance: when scheduling or suggesting activities, respect qado as the main meal and prayer times; don't suggest non-halal food or venues serving alcohol as default options.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_cuisine; https://culturalatlas.sbs.com.au/somali-culture; https://ethnomed.org/culture/somali/

knowledge.title: Khat (qaad / jaad) in Somali society: a neutral overview
knowledge.text:
Khat (Catha edulis), called qaad in the north and jaad (also "mirqaan" for the high) in the south, is a plant whose fresh leaves and stems are chewed as a stimulant. It contains cathinone and cathine, amphetamine-like substances that cause alertness, talkativeness and euphoria, followed by fatigue, insomnia or low mood. Its effect fades within a day or two of harvest, so it must be transported fresh.

Supply: almost all khat consumed in Somalia and Somaliland is imported, mainly from Ethiopia (by road, to the north and Somali Region) and from Kenya (miraa from the Meru area, flown daily into Mogadishu and other airports). Khat flights from Kenya were suspended in 2020 and resumed in 2022. The trade is large: spending on khat is a significant share of household budgets, especially in Somaliland, and khat imports are a major drain of foreign currency.

Social role: chewing (in Somali "qaad cunid" or "fadhi qaad", a chewing session) is a social activity, mostly among men, often in the afternoon in groups ("mafrish"), with tea and soft drinks, accompanied by conversation, politics and poetry. Some women also chew, and women are prominent as khat sellers in markets.

Legal status: khat is legal in Somalia, Somaliland, Djibouti, Ethiopia and Kenya. Al-Shabaab bans it in areas it controls. It is banned in many Western countries, including the United Kingdom (since 2014), the Netherlands (2013), Canada, and the United States (cathinone is a controlled substance), which affects diaspora communities. Saudi Arabia and most Gulf states ban it.

Debate: religious scholars disagree on whether khat is forbidden (xaaraam) or disliked (makruuh). Critics link heavy use to health problems (insomnia, dental and digestive problems, mental health issues), lost productivity, family conflict and spending of scarce money; defenders see it as a traditional social practice. Public campaigns against khat occur periodically.

Assistant guidance: give factual, non-judgmental information; do not encourage use; if a user wants to cut down or is worried about a relative, respond supportively and suggest health services; respect local legal differences when diaspora users ask.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khat; https://www.emcdda.europa.eu/publications/drug-profiles/khat_en

knowledge.title: Somalia's economy: overview (Dhaqaalaha Soomaaliya)
knowledge.text:
Somalia has a largely informal, private-sector-driven, dollarised economy that survived the collapse of the state in 1991 and has grown since 2012. Nominal GDP is estimated at roughly US$11–13 billion (2024–2025 estimates), or around US$600–700 per person, among the lowest in the world; growth has typically been around 3–4% a year, vulnerable to droughts, floods and insecurity. Figures vary between sources (World Bank, IMF, Somali National Bureau of Statistics), so treat them as estimates.

Main sectors:
- Livestock and pastoralism: the backbone of the rural economy and the largest export (see separate entry).
- Crop farming: sorghum, maize, sesame, beans, bananas, citrus and vegetables, mainly in the Shabeelle and Jubba valleys and the Bay region; much farmland is underused due to conflict and broken irrigation.
- Remittances from the diaspora: estimated at US$1.5–2 billion a year, around a quarter to a third of GDP.
- Services: telecommunications, mobile money, money transfer, trade (imports of food, fuel, construction materials, vehicles, electronics), real estate and construction, hotels, education and health businesses.
- Fisheries: rich but largely underexploited waters; illegal foreign fishing is a long-standing grievance.
- Frankincense and myrrh from the north-east and Sanaag.
- Emerging: offshore oil and gas exploration (agreements with Turkey's TPAO, 2024) and onshore exploration in Puntland; renewable energy, especially solar, which powers much of urban electricity through private companies.

Trade and ports: main seaports are Mogadishu (operated by Turkey's Albayrak group), Berbera (DP World, in Somaliland), Boosaaso (P&O Ports), and Kismaayo. Somalia imports most of its food staples such as rice, wheat flour, sugar and cooking oil, mostly via the UAE, Oman, India, Turkey and China.

Public finance: domestic revenue is low (a few percent of GDP), and the budget depends heavily on donor support. With IMF and World Bank programmes, Somalia reached the HIPC Completion Point in December 2023, clearing most of its external debt. It joined the East African Community in 2024, which opens trade and movement opportunities. In 2026 the Central Bank is preparing the reintroduction of new Somali shilling banknotes. US aid to the federal government was suspended in January 2026 over aid-diversion allegations (as of October 2026).

Challenges: poverty (around 70% of people live below the international poverty line by World Bank estimates), youth unemployment, climate shocks, insecurity and al-Shabaab "taxation", weak infrastructure (roads, electricity costs among the highest in Africa), and limited access to credit.

Assistant guidance: give economic figures with sources and "as of" dates; avoid confident precise numbers from memory.
Sources: https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/somalia/overview; https://www.imf.org/en/Countries/SOM; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Somalia; https://centralbank.gov.so/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Annual-Report_2025.pdf

knowledge.title: Livestock and pastoralism (Xoolaha iyo xoola-dhaqatada)
knowledge.text:
Livestock (xoolo) is central to Somali identity, economy and language. Somalis traditionally classify wealth by animals: camels (geel), cattle (lo'), sheep (ido/lax) and goats (ari). Sheep and goats together are called "ari" or "adhi". Somalia has one of the largest camel herds in the world, estimated at around 7 million or more animals, plus tens of millions of goats and sheep, and millions of cattle, mostly in the south.

Pastoral life: pastoralists (reer guuraa, xoola-dhaqato) move with their herds between seasonal grazing areas and water points (wells, berkads) according to the rains (Gu' and Dayr). Camels are herded mostly by young men and boys; women look after sheep and goats and milk processing. Agro-pastoralists combine farming and herding, especially in the Bay, Bakool and riverine areas. The nomadic hut (aqal Soomaali) is made of bent sticks and woven mats and can be packed onto camels.

The camel: the camel is the most prestigious animal. There are hundreds of Somali words for camels by age, sex, colour and condition, and camels feature in poetry, proverbs, bride-wealth (yarad) and blood compensation (mag). Camel milk (caano geel) is a staple and is increasingly sold commercially, including pasteurised milk in cities. Camel meat (hilib geel) is popular.

Exports: live animal exports are Somalia's largest source of export earnings. Millions of goats, sheep, camels and cattle are exported each year, mainly to Saudi Arabia, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Egypt, through the ports of Berbera and Boosaaso, and also via Mogadishu and Kismaayo. Exports peak in the weeks before Hajj and Eid al-Adha. Saudi import bans in the past (e.g. 1998–2009 over Rift Valley fever fears) severely hurt the economy, showing the trade's vulnerability. Somalia also exports chilled meat (by air to the Gulf), hides and skins.

Markets: large livestock markets (suuqa xoolaha) exist in Burco, Hargeysa, Gaalkacyo, Garoowe, Baydhabo, Afgooye and Kismaayo, with brokers (dilaal) negotiating prices. Prices rise sharply before Eid al-Adha.

Threats: droughts kill millions of animals (the 2020–2023 drought killed an estimated 3 million or more), pushing families into displacement camps; animal diseases; overgrazing; and loss of grazing land to enclosures. Livestock insurance and veterinary services are limited.

Assistant guidance: use correct Somali livestock terms; when users ask about prices, give current market information only from fresh sources; respect pastoral users' knowledge.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Somalia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Somalia; https://www.fao.org/somalia/en/; https://fsnau.org/

knowledge.title: Remittances and hawala (Xawaaladaha iyo lacag-dirista qurbaha)
knowledge.text:
Remittances (lacagaha qurbaha laga soo diro) from Somalis abroad are a lifeline for millions of households and a pillar of the economy, estimated at around US$1.5–2 billion a year, comparable to or larger than total foreign aid and around a quarter to a third of GDP. A large share of households, especially in cities and in Somaliland, receive regular support from relatives abroad for food, rent, school fees, medical bills and businesses.

Hawala / xawaalad: Somalis send money through money transfer operators known as hawala companies (shirkadaha xawaaladda), which grew out of a traditional trust-based system and expanded massively after 1991 when there were no banks. Major companies include Dahabshiil (founded in 1970 in Burco, one of the largest in Africa), Amal Express, Taaj, Iftin Express, Kaah Express, Juba Express, and international services like WorldRemit and others that partner with Somali operators. The sender pays cash or transfers online in, for example, the US, UK, Sweden, Canada or the Gulf; the recipient collects cash in Somalia or, increasingly, receives the money directly into a mobile money wallet (EVC Plus, Zaad, Sahal, e-Dahab, Premier Wallet).

Regulation and challenges: after 2001, Western banks became wary of Somali money transfer accounts due to anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism rules; account closures in the US, UK and Australia repeatedly threatened the flow ("de-risking"). The Central Bank of Somalia now licenses and supervises money transfer businesses and has introduced know-your-customer rules, a national payment system (2021), IBAN numbers, and the Somalia Instant Payment System (SIPS) with the SOMQR standard (launched January 2025). National ID (NIRA) verification is increasingly used for financial services.

Seasonal patterns: remittances surge during Ramadan, before Eid, during droughts and emergencies, and at the start of school years. Diaspora fundraisers (often via WhatsApp groups and mobile money) collect money for drought relief, hospital bills, mosque construction and community projects.

Practical tips an assistant can share: compare fees and exchange margins, check whether the recipient wants cash pickup or mobile wallet delivery, ensure names match ID exactly (Somali names have many spellings), and keep transaction reference numbers. Never ask users to share wallet PINs or passwords.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dahabshiil; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawala; https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/somalia/overview; https://centralbank.gov.so/news/
